stem: As a bean seed begins growing, it converts a stored polymer into separate monomers. Which statement explains the reaction that separates the subunits?

choices.text: Hydrolysis produces water when the covalent links connecting the monomers are cleaved.
Hydrolysis uses water to cleave the covalent links connecting the monomers.
Hydrolysis uses water to create covalent links connecting the monomers.
Dehydration synthesis produces water when covalent links connecting the monomers are created.

stem:
A classroom computer simulation represents a cell's supply of free monomers and polymers. Every polymer consists of four monomers connected by covalent bonds.

Simulation step | Free monomers | Polymers
0 | 48 | 0
1 | 24 | 6
2 | 0 | 12

Which statement accurately connects the changes shown in the table to the reaction occurring?

choices.text: Free monomers decrease while polymers increase; dehydration synthesis forms covalent bonds and releases water.
Free monomers decrease while polymers increase; hydrolysis forms covalent bonds and consumes water.
Free monomers decrease while polymers increase; dehydration synthesis forms covalent bonds and consumes water.
Free monomers increase while polymers decrease; hydrolysis breaks covalent bonds and consumes water.

stem:
A biodegradable coating contains biological polymer chains, each made of eight monomers connected by covalent bonds. During processing, a fixed sample of the coating gives these measurements:

Processing time (minutes) | Intact polymer chains | Unattached monomers
0 | 12 | 0
4 | 9 | 24
8 | 3 | 72

Which description connects the measured changes with the chemical reaction taking place?

choices.text: Intact chains become less numerous while unattached monomers accumulate; dehydration synthesis releases water to cleave covalent bonds.
Intact chains become less numerous while unattached monomers accumulate; hydrolysis produces water as it cleaves covalent bonds.
Intact chains become more numerous while unattached monomers disappear; dehydration synthesis releases water as it forms covalent bonds.
Intact chains become less numerous while unattached monomers accumulate; hydrolysis uses water to cleave covalent bonds.

stem:
During growth, a bacterial culture contains free monomers and polymer chains, each consisting of ten monomers connected by covalent bonds. The following measurements come from equal-sized samples of the culture.

Time (minutes) | Free monomers (millions) | Polymer chains (millions)
0 | 120 | 0
3 | 80 | 4
6 | 40 | 8

Which description correctly links the observed changes to the chemical reaction involved?

choices.text: Free monomers decline while polymer chains become more numerous; dehydration synthesis forms covalent bonds and releases water.
Free monomers decline while polymer chains become more numerous; hydrolysis forms covalent bonds and consumes water.
Free monomers decline while polymer chains become more numerous; dehydration synthesis forms covalent bonds and consumes water.
Free monomers become more numerous while polymer chains decline; hydrolysis breaks covalent bonds and consumes water.

stem: A laboratory sample initially contains two linear polymer chains, each composed of five monomers. One treatment hydrolyzes exactly five bonds connecting monomers in these chains. A second treatment then causes exactly two dehydration synthesis reactions, each joining two separate fragments. No other bonds form or break. Relative to the initial sample, how many separate polymer-derived molecules remain, and what is the net change in water molecules?

choices.text: Five polymer-derived molecules remain; seven water molecules are consumed overall.
Five polymer-derived molecules remain; three water molecules are released overall.
Five polymer-derived molecules remain; three water molecules are consumed overall.
Three polymer-derived molecules remain; three water molecules are consumed overall.

stem: In a bacterial cell, a linear polymer chain of six monomers is lengthened when five free monomers are added to its end one at a time by dehydration synthesis. An enzyme then hydrolyzes exactly four of the bonds linking monomers in the lengthened chain, and no other bonds form or break. Compared with the moment before lengthening began, how many separate molecules come from the chain, and what is the net water change?

choices.text: Five separate molecules from the chain; one water molecule released overall.
Five separate molecules from the chain; nine water molecules released overall.
Five separate molecules from the chain; one water molecule consumed overall.
Four separate molecules from the chain; one water molecule released overall.

stem: A plant cell starts with fifteen free monomers and uses dehydration synthesis to assemble them into three separate linear chains of five monomers each. An enzyme then hydrolyzes exactly four monomer-linking bonds, chosen anywhere among the three chains. No other bonds form or break. Compared with the fifteen free monomers at the start, how many separate molecules result, and what is the net change in water molecules?

choices.text: Seven separate molecules; eight water molecules released overall.
Seven separate molecules; sixteen water molecules released overall.
Seven separate molecules; eight water molecules consumed overall.
Four separate molecules; eight water molecules released overall.

stem: Researchers apply a treatment to pear skin that breaks down cellulose in its cell walls without changing the amount of stored starch. The treated skin is easier to puncture than untreated skin. Which explanation best connects cellulose's structure and function to this result?

choices.text: Cellulose is the main energy-storage carbohydrate in pear cells, so its breakdown leaves the skin without stored fuel to maintain its strength.
Cellulose is a single sugar molecule used for immediate energy, so its breakdown prevents pear cells from fueling wall maintenance.
Cellulose consists of many sugar monomers covalently joined into chains that reinforce cell walls, so breaking down those chains reduces the skin's strength.
Cellulose is a protein made of folded amino acid chains, so its breakdown destroys the protein framework supporting the pear skin.

stem: A textile company spins cotton fibers into thread that resists breaking when pulled. The fiber walls contain abundant cellulose. Which statement best connects cellulose’s structure and function to the strength of the thread?

choices.text: Cellulose stores energy in cotton fibers, and this stored fuel gives the thread its resistance to breaking.
Cellulose contains many glucose units covalently joined into long, linear chains that provide structural reinforcement in the cotton fiber walls.
Cellulose is a single sugar molecule that supplies quick energy, allowing cotton fibers to resist pulling.
Cellulose consists of folded amino acid chains whose protein structure reinforces the cotton fibers.

stem: During spring growth, a maple tree uses much of the starch stored in its trunk, but the cellulose-rich walls of its cells continue to provide structural support. Which statement best explains why this support persists?

choices.text: Cellulose provides support by serving as the tree’s main energy-storage polysaccharide after the starch supply decreases.
Cellulose is a single sugar molecule that supplies quick energy for maintaining the tree’s supporting walls.
Cellulose contains glucose units covalently joined into long, linear polysaccharide chains that reinforce cell walls independently of stored starch.
Cellulose consists of folded amino acid chains whose protein fibers maintain the strength of the tree’s cell walls.

stem: A student makes starch-based packaging panels and asks whether adding cellulose increases their ability to support a load without bending. The student can prepare mixtures with or without added cellulose and mold them into panels. Which procedure would best answer the question?

choices.text: Prepare multiple panels with and without added cellulose, keeping panel dimensions and drying conditions identical, and compare the loads needed to bend them by a fixed amount.
Prepare multiple panels with and without added cellulose, keeping panel dimensions and drying conditions identical, and compare the amounts of starch present.
Prepare thick panels with added cellulose and thin panels without it, keeping drying conditions identical, and compare the loads needed to bend them by a fixed amount.
Prepare multiple identical panels containing added cellulose, keep drying conditions identical, and calculate the average load needed to bend them by a fixed amount.

stem: A textile scientist investigates whether cellulose gives starch-coated cotton yarn resistance to breaking. The scientist has a solution that selectively removes cellulose but leaves starch unchanged. Which procedure would most directly test cellulose’s structural contribution?

choices.text: Divide yarn pieces of identical length and thickness from one batch randomly between the cellulose-removing solution and a matching solution lacking the removing agent, then measure the starch remaining on each piece.
Place thin yarn pieces in the cellulose-removing solution and thick pieces of the same length in a matching solution lacking the removing agent, then measure the force needed to break each piece.
Place every yarn piece of identical length and thickness from one batch in the cellulose-removing solution, then measure the force needed to break each piece and report the mean.

Divide yarn pieces of identical length and thickness from one batch randomly between the cellulose-removing solution and a matching solution lacking the removing agent, then measure the force needed to break each piece.

stem: A museum conservator asks whether cellulose helps starch-coated repair paper resist puncturing. A solution can remove cellulose while leaving the starch intact. Which procedure would best isolate cellulose’s contribution to the paper’s strength?

choices.text: Randomly divide equally thick pieces from one batch between the cellulose-removing solution and a matching solution without the removal agent, then measure the starch remaining in each piece.
Randomly divide equally thick pieces from one batch between the cellulose-removing solution and a matching solution without the removal agent, then measure the force needed to puncture each piece.
Expose thin pieces to the cellulose-removing solution and thicker pieces from the same batch to a matching solution without the removal agent, then measure puncture force.
Expose equally thick pieces from one batch to the cellulose-removing solution, then measure their puncture forces and report the mean.

stem: Researchers maintain harvested potato tuber tissue with a steady supply of glucose. A treatment selectively prevents glucose monomers from being joined into starch, but glucose availability and cellulose assembly remain unchanged. Compared with untreated tissue, which outcome is best supported?

choices.text: The treated tissue will accumulate less starch for energy storage, while its cellulose-based structural support remains largely unaffected.
The treated tissue will lose structural support because starch is the principal polysaccharide that strengthens plant cell walls.
The treated tissue will maintain normal carbohydrate energy storage because cellulose can replace starch wherever glucose polymers are needed.
The treated tissue will lack glucose for immediate energy use because blocking starch assembly prevents glucose from being produced.

stem: Wheat leaves normally accumulate starch during daylight. Researchers develop a wheat line in which glucose monomers cannot be joined into starch. Measurements show that glucose production and the assembly of cellulose remain normal. Compared with ordinary wheat, which change is best predicted in these leaves?

choices.text: Their structural support will decrease, because starch is the main polysaccharide supporting plant cell walls.
Their capacity to store energy as starch will decrease, while cellulose-based structural support will remain largely unchanged.
Their carbohydrate energy storage will remain unchanged, because cellulose can replace starch whenever glucose monomers are available.
Their supply of glucose for immediate energy use will disappear, because preventing starch assembly also prevents glucose production.

stem: A herbicide is applied to the growing root tips of young corn plants. It blocks the enzyme that links glucose monomers into cellulose. Glucose from the leaves still reaches the root cells at normal levels, and the enzyme that links glucose into starch in those cells is unaffected. Which prediction about the treated root cells is best supported?

choices.text: The root cells will lose their stored energy reserves, because cellulose is the polysaccharide plants use to store glucose.
Newly built cell walls in the root tips will be structurally weak, while the root cells will continue to build starch reserves.
The root cell walls will remain sturdy, because starch is built from the same glucose monomers and can replace cellulose in the wall.
The root cells will be starved of glucose for energy, because the herbicide prevents glucose from being made.

stem: A bakery tests a modified canola oil in which some carbon–carbon double bonds in the fatty acid chains have been converted to single bonds. The chain lengths remain unchanged. Which prediction best connects this modification to the oil’s texture at room temperature?

choices.text: The oil tends to become firmer because fewer kinks allow the fatty acid chains to pack more tightly.
The oil tends to become firmer because the chains become more unsaturated, and unsaturated chains contain only single carbon–carbon bonds.
The oil tends to become softer because removing double bonds introduces kinks that prevent tight packing.
The oil tends to become firmer because converting double bonds to single bonds changes the chains from hydrophilic to hydrophobic.

stem: A cosmetics manufacturer needs a fat that flows easily at room temperature for use in a skin lotion. The available fats have fatty acid chains of comparable lengths but differ in saturation. Which recommendation best explains how to obtain the desired consistency?

choices.text: Select a fat rich in unsaturated fatty acids because these chains have only single carbon–carbon bonds, which create bends.
Select a fat rich in unsaturated fatty acids because double bonds straighten the chains and promote close packing.
Select a fat rich in unsaturated fatty acids because double bonds bend the chains and reduce tight packing.
Select a fat rich in unsaturated fatty acids because double bonds make the chains hydrophilic and therefore liquid.

stem: An agricultural laboratory examines oils extracted from sunflower seeds grown in two fields. The northern field’s oil contains a higher proportion of unsaturated fatty acids than the southern field’s oil, while fatty acid chain lengths are similar. Which prediction about the northern field’s oil at room temperature is best supported by its fatty acid structure?

choices.text: It should be more likely to remain liquid because unsaturated fatty acids have only single carbon–carbon bonds that create kinks.
It should be more likely to become solid because double bonds straighten fatty acid chains and promote tight packing.
It should be more likely to remain liquid because double bonds make fatty acid chains hydrophilic.
It should be more likely to remain liquid because double bonds create kinks that reduce tight packing of fatty acid chains.

stem:
A bakery tests three fat blends to find one that stays mostly liquid at 20°C. The fatty acid chains are equal in length across the blends. Measurements at 20°C give these results:

Blend | Average carbon–carbon double bonds per fatty acid chain | Percentage of fat that is liquid
P | 0 | 0%
Q | 1 | 60%
R | 2 | 100%

Which statement accurately describes the pattern and connects it to fatty acid structure?

choices.text: As double bonds become more numerous, the liquid percentage increases because kinked fatty acid chains cannot pack as closely.
As double bonds become more numerous, the liquid percentage decreases because unsaturated fatty acid chains are straight and pack tightly.
As double bonds become more numerous, the liquid percentage increases because the fats become hydrophilic.
As double bonds become more numerous, the liquid percentage increases because the fatty acid chains become more saturated.

stem:
A skin-care company is selecting a fat blend for a lotion stored at cool temperatures. All fatty acid chains in the blends have the same length, and each unsaturated chain contains one carbon–carbon double bond. The company obtains these measurements:

Blend | Saturated fatty acid chains (%) | Melting temperature (°C)
Rose | 20 | 5
Fern | 50 | 18
Moss | 80 | 32

Which statement correctly summarizes the measured relationship and connects it to fatty acid structure?

choices.text: Blends with a greater percentage of saturated chains melt at lower temperatures because saturated chains have more kinks.
Blends with a greater percentage of saturated chains melt at higher temperatures because saturation makes fats hydrophilic.
Blends with a greater percentage of saturated chains melt at higher temperatures because saturated chains contain more carbon–carbon double bonds.
Blends with a greater percentage of saturated chains melt at higher temperatures because straighter chains can pack more closely.

stem:
An animal-feed supplier needs a fat that remains solid in a cool warehouse. Three candidate fats have equal-length fatty acid chains but differ in their degree of unsaturation. Testing produces the following measurements:

Fat | Average carbon–carbon double bonds per fatty acid chain | Melting temperature (°C)
Cedar | 3 | −12
Maple | 2 | 8
Pine | 0 | 48

As the average number of double bonds decreases, which statement describes the measured trend and explains its structural basis?

choices.text: Melting temperature falls because fatty acid chains with fewer double bonds have more kinks and pack less closely.
Melting temperature rises because fatty acid chains with fewer double bonds make the fats hydrophilic.
Melting temperature rises because fatty acid chains with fewer double bonds are more unsaturated.
Melting temperature rises because fatty acid chains with fewer kinks can pack together more closely.

stem: Researchers develop a soybean variety that produces seed storage fats with a greater proportion of saturated fatty acids than the original variety. Both varieties store the same mass of fat, and their fatty acid chains have the same lengths. When the seeds are compared at the same temperature, which prediction best connects the altered fatty acid composition to the properties and function of the fats?

choices.text: The new variety’s storage fats will tend to be less liquid but will retain their role as an energy reserve.
The new variety’s storage fats will tend to be more liquid but will retain their role as an energy reserve.
The new variety’s storage fats will tend to be less liquid and become water-soluble, losing their role as an energy reserve.
The new variety’s storage fats will tend to be less liquid and assemble into phospholipid bilayers, replacing their role as an energy reserve.

stem: A mutation in a freshwater alga causes the fatty acids in its stored oil droplets to carry more carbon–carbon double bonds per chain than in nonmutant cells. The mutant and nonmutant cells store equal masses of oil, and chain lengths are identical. If both are kept at the same temperature, what is the most likely effect of the mutation on the stored oil?

choices.text: The oil will tend to be more solid, and it will still function as a stored energy reserve.
The oil will tend to be more fluid and will dissolve into the watery cytoplasm, so it can no longer be stored.
The oil will tend to be more fluid and will assemble into membrane bilayers instead of being stored.
The oil will tend to be more fluid, and it will still function as a stored energy reserve.

stem: A soil fungus exposed to a new growth condition replaces some saturated fatty acids in its stored fats with unsaturated fatty acids. Measurements show no change in total stored-fat mass or fatty acid chain length. Compared with reserves produced under the original condition, what change in the properties and function of these fats is most likely at an identical temperature?

choices.text: The reserves become more liquid but remain hydrophobic fats that store energy.
The reserves become less liquid but remain hydrophobic fats that store energy.
The reserves become more liquid and dissolve in water, losing their energy-storage role.
The reserves become more liquid and assemble into phospholipid bilayers, replacing their energy-storage role.

stem: A researcher synthesizes two RNA molecules, each 30 nucleotides long. Each contains exactly 9 adenines, 6 uracils, 8 guanines, and 7 cytosines, but the bases are arranged in a different order in each molecule. What best explains whether these two RNA molecules could carry different genetic messages?

choices.text: They must carry the same message, because each molecule is built from 30 nucleotides.
They must carry the same message, because both contain identical numbers of A, U, G, and C.
They must carry the same message, because both share the same repeating ribose-phosphate backbone.
They could carry different messages, because the information in a nucleic acid is determined by the sequence of its bases.

stem: A laboratory technician revises the design of a synthetic RNA strand by swapping the positions of an adenine nucleotide and a cytosine nucleotide. No nucleotides are added or removed, and all other positions stay the same. What is the potential effect on the information encoded by the strand?

choices.text: The encoded information must remain unchanged because the strand still has the same length.
The encoded information must remain unchanged because the strand retains the same number of each base.
The encoded information must remain unchanged because the strand retains its repeating sugar-phosphate backbone.
The encoded information can change because the rearrangement changes the nucleotide sequence.

stem: A student compares a short DNA segment from a mouse with one from a fruit fly. One strand of each segment is 12 nucleotides long and contains 3 adenines, 3 thymines, 3 guanines, and 3 cytosines, but the bases appear in a different order in each strand. Which statement best explains whether these segments could carry different biological instructions?

choices.text: They must carry the same instructions, because each strand is exactly 12 nucleotides long.
They must carry the same instructions, because each strand has three of every base.
They must carry the same instructions, because both strands are built on the same sugar-phosphate backbone.
They could carry different instructions, because the information in DNA depends on the sequence in which the bases occur along the strand.

stem: A team developing a DNA-based sensor attaches 24-nucleotide DNA tags to beads. Adding complementary DNA strands produces base pairing, measured as the percentage of tags bound to an added strand. The team asks whether binding requires a matching base order rather than simply an added strand containing the same quantities of A, T, C, and G. Which comparison treatment best addresses this question? Unless a change is specified, strand concentration and all other experimental conditions remain unchanged.

choices.text: Add complementary 24-nucleotide RNA strands containing uracil instead of thymine.
Add the complementary DNA strands at three times their original concentration.
Test the DNA-tagged beads without adding any second strands.
Add 24-nucleotide DNA strands with the same base counts as the complementary strands but a noncomplementary sequence.

stem: Students are investigating the assembly of pairs of synthetic RNA strands, each 20 nucleotides long. They add an antiparallel, complementary RNA partner to a starting RNA strand and count the paired molecules formed. They want to determine whether pairing requires complementary nucleotide order rather than simply a partner containing particular quantities of each base. Which control treatment best isolates nucleotide order? All conditions remain unchanged unless a choice specifies otherwise.

choices.text: Replace the partner with an RNA strand of equal length and identical base counts, but with a noncomplementary base order.
Replace the partner with a complementary DNA strand containing thymine instead of uracil.
Keep the complementary RNA partner but add it at three times its original concentration.
Test the starting RNA strand without adding any partner strand.

stem: A materials laboratory uses DNA strands to fasten two thin sheets together. One sheet carries 18-nucleotide single-stranded DNA connectors; the other carries antiparallel, complementary DNA strands. Researchers measure the percentage of connectors paired with strands on the second sheet. They want to determine whether pairing requires complementary nucleotide order rather than merely the same collection of bases. Which comparison treatment best isolates this variable? Apart from the stated change, strand amounts and experimental conditions remain constant.

choices.text: Replace the second sheet’s strands with complementary RNA strands containing uracil instead of thymine.
Place twice as many of the original complementary DNA strands on the second sheet.
Use a second sheet with no nucleic acid strands attached.
Replace the second sheet’s strands with DNA strands of equal length and identical base counts, arranged in a noncomplementary sequence.

stem: A researcher redesigns a double-stranded DNA identification tag to distinguish two sample batches. The strand used to build the redesigned tag originally reads 5′-TGCATGAC-3′; the researcher substitutes A for the sixth nucleotide, G, leaving every other position unchanged. Predict the sequence of a DNA strand synthesized complementary to the redesigned strand, reported in the 5′→3′ direction.

choices.text: 5′-ACGTATTG-3′
5′-GUUAUGCA-3′
5′-GTTATGCA-3′
5′-GTCATGCA-3′

stem: A botanist finds that a DNA strand in one seedling reads 5′-GATCCAG-3′. In a second seedling, the corresponding strand differs only at position 2, where G replaces A. If a new DNA strand is synthesized complementary to the second seedling’s strand, what sequence will it have when read 5′→3′?

choices.text: 5′-CCAGGTC-3′
5′-CUGGACC-3′
5′-CTGGATC-3′
5′-CTGGACC-3′

stem: An artificial DNA molecule stores information for a digital archive. During an update, a technician changes the seventh nucleotide of a strand from A to G without altering any other position. Before the update, that strand reads 5′-CTAGGCAT-3′. What sequence is predicted for a new DNA strand synthesized complementary to the updated strand, written 5′→3′?

choices.text: 5′-GATCCGCA-3′
5′-ACGCCUAG-3′
5′-ACGCCTAG-3′
5′-ATGCCTAG-3′

stem: Scientists compare single-chain oxygen-binding proteins from two fish species. The proteins contain the same number and types of amino acids, but some amino acids occur in different positions. The proteins fold differently, and one binds oxygen less effectively. Which explanation best accounts for this difference in function?

choices.text: The proteins have identical primary structures because their chains are equally long, so primary structure cannot explain the binding difference.
Peptide bonds alone control protein folding, so differences in R-group positions cannot account for the binding difference.
The different amino acid orders can change R-group interactions, altering the folded shape and the ability to bind oxygen.
The proteins differ in quaternary structure because that level describes the three-dimensional shape of each individual chain.

stem: A laboratory designs two proteins for a coating that holds a dye. Each protein is a single polypeptide containing 60 amino acids. Their sequences differ at four positions, where the amino acids have different R-group properties. Tests reveal different three-dimensional shapes and weaker dye binding by one protein. Which explanation best connects the sequence differences to the binding results?

choices.text: Equal chain lengths establish identical primary structures, so amino acid sequences cannot account for the unequal dye binding.
Peptide bonds alone control each protein’s folded shape, so differences in R groups cannot account for the unequal dye binding.
The different folds indicate different quaternary structures because quaternary structure describes the overall shape of an individual polypeptide.
Differences in R-group interactions can produce different folds, changing how effectively each protein binds the dye.

stem: A bacterial protein made of one polypeptide helps cells attach to surfaces. Researchers test two forms, each containing 80 amino acids. The forms differ in the order of amino acids within one short section. They have different folded shapes, and one supports weaker attachment. What best explains these results?

choices.text: Both forms have the same primary structure because each contains 80 amino acids, so their sequences cannot account for weaker attachment.
Peptide bonds alone establish the folded shape, so rearranging amino acids cannot account for weaker attachment.
The different amino acid order can alter R-group interactions, changing the folded shape and its ability to support attachment.
The altered fold represents a change in quaternary structure because that level describes the shape of one polypeptide.

stem:
A laboratory evaluates two forms of a structural protein used as an elastic spring. Each molecule is a single, unbroken polypeptide of 150 amino acids. Only the amino acid at position 65 differs between the forms. Under the same testing conditions, researchers measure folded shape and the greatest extension from which each molecule returns to its starting shape.

Protein form | R group at position 65 | Folded shape | Greatest reversible extension (nm)
Initial | Uncharged and hydrophilic | Compact | 4
Altered | Hydrophobic | Less compact | 9

Which conclusion best connects the observed pattern to protein structure and function?

choices.text: The altered form has a less compact fold and greater reversible extension, consistent with changed R-group interactions affecting its elasticity.
The forms have the same primary structure because both contain 150 amino acids, so their different elasticity cannot be associated with a sequence difference.
The altered form stretches farther because the R-group replacement breaks peptide bonds, producing a shorter polypeptide.
The less compact fold is a change in quaternary structure that accounts for the altered form’s greater reversible extension.

stem:
A materials laboratory tests two forms of a structural protein that helps a soft gel withstand compression. Every protein molecule contains a single, unbroken polypeptide of 180 amino acids. The forms differ only at amino acid position 72. Gels containing equal amounts of either form are tested under the same conditions.

Protein form | R group at position 72 | Overall folded shape | Maximum force supported before gel collapses (N)
Standard | Charged | Compact | 8
Replacement | Uncharged and hydrophilic | Less compact | 3

Which interpretation connects the measured relationship to protein structure and function?

choices.text: The forms have the same primary structure because both contain 180 amino acids, so their different performance cannot involve an amino acid sequence difference.
The replacement form is less compact and supports less force, consistent with altered R-group interactions changing folding and structural support.
The replacement form supports less force because the R-group change breaks backbone peptide bonds, producing a shorter protein.
The replacement form supports less force because its less compact folding indicates a change in quaternary structure.

stem:
A team studies two forms of an antifreeze protein from an Arctic fish. Each molecule is a single, unbroken polypeptide of 120 amino acids, and the forms differ only in the amino acid at position 28. Both forms are tested at the same temperature, pH, and concentration.

Protein form | R group at position 28 | Folded shape | Reduction in ice crystal growth (%)
Native | Uncharged and hydrophilic | Reference shape | 85
Variant | Hydrophobic | Altered from reference | 15

Which statement best describes the pattern in the data and links it to protein structure and function?

choices.text: Both forms have the same primary structure because each contains 120 amino acids, so the drop in activity cannot come from a sequence change.
The variant reduces ice growth less because the new R group breaks peptide bonds, leaving a shorter polypeptide.
The variant's altered folded shape reflects a change in quaternary structure, which explains its weaker ice-growth reduction.
The variant has an altered folded shape and much weaker ice-growth reduction, consistent with a changed R group altering folding interactions and thus function.

stem: A single-chain protein used in an elastic material returns to its original shape after gentle stretching. An ionic interaction between two R groups helps stabilize its folded form. Researchers produce a version in which one of these charged amino acids is replaced by an amino acid with a nonpolar R group; chain length and peptide-bond connectivity are unchanged. Which prediction best explains how this replacement could affect the protein’s shape recovery?

choices.text: Unchanged peptide-bond connectivity preserves primary structure, so the protein must retain its original shape recovery.
The replacement directly changes secondary structure, which is defined by ionic interactions between R groups, impairing shape recovery.
Loss of the ionic interaction may alter tertiary folding, making the protein less able to recover its original shape.
The replacement disrupts quaternary structure by separating polypeptide subunits, preventing the protein from recovering its original shape.

stem: A structural protein in a marine animal consists of one polypeptide, and its compact folded form is required to provide support. Two oppositely charged R groups help stabilize this form through an ionic interaction. Researchers replace one of these amino acids so that the two R groups now have the same charge. The number of amino acids and all peptide-bond connections are retained. Which prediction best explains how this replacement could affect structural support?

choices.text: The changed R-group interaction may alter tertiary folding, making the protein less able to provide structural support.
Preserving the peptide-bond connections keeps the primary structure identical, so the protein must retain its shape and supporting function.
The replacement directly changes secondary structure because ionic interactions between R groups define that level, potentially weakening structural support.
The replacement may weaken structural support by disrupting quaternary structure and causing the protein's polypeptide subunits to separate.

stem: An experimental adhesive contains a protein made of one polypeptide chain. The protein must retain a particular folded shape for the adhesive to hold surfaces together. A polar R group forms a hydrogen bond with another R group elsewhere in the chain. Researchers replace the first amino acid with one having a nonpolar R group, without changing the number of amino acids or their peptide-bond connectivity. Which prediction best explains a possible effect on adhesion?

choices.text: Unchanged peptide-bond connectivity means the primary structure is unchanged, so the protein must retain its adhesive function.
Loss of the R-group hydrogen bond directly changes secondary structure, because secondary structure is defined by hydrogen bonds between R groups.
The replacement may disrupt an R-group interaction, altering tertiary folding and weakening the protein’s adhesive function.
Loss of the R-group hydrogen bond separates polypeptide subunits, disrupting quaternary structure and weakening adhesion.

stem: A food-processing laboratory compares two fungal enzymes that might catalyze the conversion of a sugar into a product. The enzymes have active sites of similar size but with different shapes and charge distributions. Under matched conditions, enzyme M accelerates the conversion, whereas enzyme N does not. Which explanation best connects enzyme structure to the observed reaction rates?

choices.text: The sugar is compatible with M’s active site but not N’s, enabling M to donate the energy needed for the conversion.
The sugar is compatible with M’s active site but not N’s, enabling M to decrease the activation energy for the conversion.
The sugar is compatible with M’s active site but not N’s, enabling M to increase the activation energy for the conversion.
The sugar is compatible with both active sites because they are similar in size, enabling both enzymes to accelerate the conversion.

stem:
A water-treatment facility evaluates an enzyme additive that converts dissolved compounds into products. For each compound, paired water samples have the same starting concentration and reaction conditions, except that only one receives the enzyme. Initial rates of product formation are recorded below.

Compound | No enzyme added | Enzyme added
M | 3 units/min | 3 units/min
N | 4 units/min | 24 units/min

Which explanation best relates the measurements to the biological principles of enzyme action?

choices.text: The enzyme transfers energy to compound N, causing products to form more rapidly.
Compound N binds at the active site, where the enzyme increases the reaction’s activation energy.
Compound N can bind appropriately at the enzyme’s active site, enabling catalysis that lowers the reaction’s activation energy.
The enzyme reduces activation energy for both compounds because active sites can catalyze reactions with every substrate.

stem:
A food-processing laboratory tests a starch-digesting enzyme extracted from barley under several temperature treatments. All reaction mixtures have the same pH and starting concentrations of enzyme and starch. For the heat-treatment trial, the enzyme is held at 65°C and then cooled to 40°C before fresh starch is supplied.

Temperature treatment | Initial reaction rate (relative units)
20°C | 4
40°C | 16
65°C | 1
65°C, then cooled to 40°C | 16

Which interpretation connects these observations to the effects of temperature on enzyme structure and activity?

choices.text: Activity rises throughout the tested temperature range because increasing temperature always improves the enzyme’s fit with starch.
Heating the enzyme to 65°C causes permanent denaturation, preventing activity from returning when the sample cools.
Heating to 65°C separates the enzyme’s amino acids by breaking peptide bonds, and cooling reconnects those amino acids.
The greatest measured activity occurs at 40°C, and activity restored after cooling supports a reversible alteration of enzyme shape.

stem: A laundry detergent contains a protein-digesting enzyme whose optimal temperature is 40°C. The wash setting is switched to 75°C without changing pH or the starting concentrations of enzyme and protein substrate. Measurements at 75°C reveal disrupted hydrogen bonding and distortion of the enzyme’s active site. How should the initial rate of protein breakdown compare with the rate at 40°C, and why?

choices.text: Protein breakdown should slow because the distorted active site interacts less effectively with the substrate.
Protein breakdown should accelerate because every temperature increase makes enzyme–substrate collisions more frequent and productive.
Protein breakdown should proceed at the same rate because the enzyme’s amino acid sequence remains intact.
Protein breakdown should proceed at the same rate because the enzyme is not used up while catalyzing reactions.

stem: A growing plant cell builds a biological polymer from monomers. This synthesis requires an energy input and is coupled to ATP hydrolysis. How does ATP support polymer synthesis?

choices.text: ATP hydrolysis generates new energy that the cell uses to assemble the polymer.
Polymer assembly releases energy that the cell uses to synthesize ATP.
ATP provides energy for polymer assembly without undergoing any chemical change.
ATP hydrolysis releases chemical energy that can be used to drive the energy-requiring assembly of the polymer.

stem: A yeast cell uses a membrane protein to move an uncharged solute against its concentration gradient, powered by coupled ATP hydrolysis. A treatment disconnects ATP hydrolysis from transport without altering the protein's catalytic activity. During the observation, ATP concentration, the solute gradient, and the ATP hydrolysis rate are maintained; no replacement energy source is coupled to transport. What immediate effect on uphill solute transport is expected, and why?

choices.text: Uphill transport slows because ATP hydrolysis no longer supplies energy through coupling to the transport process.
Uphill transport proceeds at its previous rate because ATP hydrolysis elsewhere automatically provides the energy for transport.
Uphill transport proceeds at its previous rate because the protein's catalytic activity removes the need for energy input.
Uphill transport slows because ATP hydrolysis consumes energy that would otherwise power solute movement.

stem: A student places spinach leaf disks in a bicarbonate solution and exposes them to three light levels, holding CO₂ supply and temperature constant. After rates stabilize, the student records outputs in relative units per minute. Full light: oxygen release 9, sugar formation 6. Partial shade: oxygen release 6, sugar formation 4. Deep shade: oxygen release 3, sugar formation 2. Which statement correctly describes these results and explains them using the roles of the two photosynthetic stages?

choices.text: Both outputs decrease as light dims; the light reactions in the thylakoids directly build sugar, so less light means less sugar.
Both outputs decrease as light dims; the oxygen comes from CO₂ broken apart during the Calvin cycle, which slows in dim light.
Both outputs decrease as light dims; less light means the light reactions make less ATP and NADPH, which limits sugar formation by the Calvin cycle in the stroma.
Both outputs decrease as light dims; the Calvin cycle supplies ATP and NADPH that power the light reactions, so both stages slow together.

stem: A researcher supplies CO₂ to a green alga growing under a lamp. Which explanation connects the absorbed light energy to the incorporation of the supplied carbon into carbohydrates inside the alga’s chloroplast?

choices.text: Light reactions in the stroma generate ATP and NADPH, which the Calvin cycle at the thylakoid membranes uses to build carbohydrates from the supplied CO₂.
Light reactions at the thylakoid membranes generate ATP and NADPH, which the Calvin cycle in the stroma uses to build carbohydrates from the supplied CO₂.
The Calvin cycle in the stroma generates ATP and NADPH, which power light reactions at the thylakoid membranes as the supplied CO₂ becomes carbohydrates.
The Calvin cycle absorbs light in the stroma to build carbohydrates from the supplied CO₂ without using ATP or NADPH from the light reactions.

stem:
A microbiologist investigates ATP production in cultures of an aerobic bacterium as dissolved oxygen becomes less available. Each culture contains the same number of cells and receives the same glucose supply. Temperature and pH remain unchanged.

Dissolved oxygen (µmol/L) | ATP production rate (nmol/min)
18 | 30
6 | 14
0 | 2

Which explanation connects the observed ATP production pattern to oxygen’s function in cellular respiration?

choices.text: Across the measured conditions, ATP production falls as oxygen availability decreases because oxygen directly combines ADP with phosphate to produce ATP.
Across the measured conditions, ATP production falls as oxygen availability decreases because oxygen supplies electrons to the electron transport chain.
Across the measured conditions, ATP production falls as oxygen availability decreases because oxygen receives electrons at the end of the electron transport chain.
Across the measured conditions, ATP production falls as oxygen availability decreases because glycolysis needs oxygen to produce ATP.

stem: A culture of aerobic bacteria is growing with glucose and oxygen available. A compound is added that carries H⁺ back across the bacterial plasma membrane into the cytoplasm by a route that bypasses ATP synthase. The compound does not directly inhibit glycolysis or the electron transport chain. Which prediction best describes the short-term effect on the bacteria's ATP production?

choices.text: Oxidative phosphorylation makes more ATP because protons now return across the membrane more rapidly.
ATP made by oxidative phosphorylation drops, while glycolysis in the cytoplasm continues to make ATP.
Oxidative phosphorylation is unaffected because ATP synthase uses energy delivered directly by oxygen.
The cells stop making ATP entirely because glycolysis is powered by the same proton gradient.

stem: A protist cell growing in a pond is modeled as a cube. It absorbs oxygen through all six faces. Its edge length grows from 2 μm to 6 μm. Use surface area = 6s² and volume = s³, where s is edge length. The maximum oxygen absorption rate per square micrometer of surface stays the same. The oxygen demand per cubic micrometer of cytoplasm also stays the same. Compared with the smaller cell, how does the larger cell's maximum oxygen uptake per unit volume change, and what does this mean for meeting its oxygen demand?

choices.text: It triples, so the cell is better able to meet its oxygen demand.
It increases ninefold, so the cell is better able to meet its oxygen demand.
It stays the same, so the cell's ability to meet its oxygen demand is unchanged.
It falls to one-third of its original value, so the cell is less able to meet its oxygen demand.

stem: A growing yeast cell is represented by a sphere that releases waste across its entire outer surface. Its radius increases from 3 μm to 12 μm. For this model, surface area = 4πr² and volume = 4πr³/3, with r representing radius. The maximum waste removal rate per unit surface area stays fixed, as does waste production per unit volume. How does growth affect the maximum waste removal rate per unit volume and the cell’s capacity to keep pace with waste production?

choices.text: It rises fourfold, increasing the capacity to keep pace with waste production.
It rises 16-fold, increasing the capacity to keep pace with waste production.
It falls to one-quarter of its original value, reducing the capacity to keep pace with waste production.
It stays constant, leaving the capacity to keep pace with waste production unchanged.

stem: A researcher represents a growing animal cell as a cube to examine its ability to release heat through its entire outer surface. The cube’s edge length increases from 4 μm to 20 μm. For edge length x, use surface area = 6x² and volume = x³. Assume that maximum heat release per unit surface area stays fixed and heat production per unit volume also stays fixed. How does growth change maximum heat release per unit volume and the cell’s capacity to keep pace with heat production?

choices.text: It rises to five times the original value, increasing the capacity to keep pace with heat production.
It falls to one-fifth of the original value, reducing the capacity to keep pace with heat production.
It rises to 25 times the original value, increasing the capacity to keep pace with heat production.
It stays at the original value, leaving the capacity to keep pace with heat production unchanged.

stem:
A biologist compares two strains of a single-celled protist that absorb glucose from the water around them. One strain has a smooth surface; the other has many fingerlike membrane projections, all exposed to the water.

Strain | Membrane surface area (μm²) | Volume (μm³)
Smooth | 900 | 1,500
Projections | 2,700 | 1,500

In both strains, each square micrometer of membrane absorbs glucose at the same maximum rate, and each cubic micrometer of cytoplasm needs the same amount of glucose. Which claim about the membrane projections do these data best support?

choices.text: The projections do not change maximum glucose uptake, because two cells of equal volume have equal ability to absorb glucose.
The projections lower maximum glucose uptake, because a larger surface area-to-volume ratio makes exchange with the environment less efficient.
The projections triple glucose demand but leave maximum uptake unchanged, because demand depends on membrane area and uptake depends on volume.
The projections triple maximum glucose uptake while glucose demand stays the same, because they add absorbing surface without adding cell volume.

stem:
Scientists investigate whether an elongated shape improves oxygen exchange in cultured animal cells. They collect the following measurements, with all plasma membrane surfaces exposed to the surrounding liquid.

Cell shape | Membrane surface area (μm²) | Volume (μm³)
Rounded | 1,000 | 2,000
Elongated | 1,500 | 2,000

Maximum oxygen uptake per unit membrane area is identical in both shapes, as is oxygen demand per unit cell volume. Which claim about the elongated shape is supported by these measurements?

choices.text: The elongated shape leaves maximum oxygen uptake unchanged, because equal cell volumes provide equal capacities for oxygen exchange.
The elongated shape increases maximum oxygen uptake by 50% while leaving oxygen demand unchanged, because it provides more membrane area at the same volume.
The elongated shape decreases maximum oxygen uptake, because its higher surface area-to-volume ratio makes oxygen exchange less efficient.
The elongated shape increases oxygen demand by 50% without changing maximum oxygen uptake, because demand follows membrane area while uptake follows volume.

stem:
A laboratory compares waste removal in two bacterial strains with different cell shapes. The entire measured membrane surface is available for exchange with the environment.

Cell shape | Membrane surface area (μm²) | Cell volume (μm³)
Compact | 12 | 2
Flattened | 24 | 2

The strains have identical maximum waste-removal rates per unit membrane area and identical waste-production rates per unit cell volume. Which claim about the flattened cells is best supported by the measurements?

choices.text: Flattened cells have unchanged maximum waste-removal capacity, because their volume equals that of compact cells.
Flattened cells have twice the maximum waste-removal capacity but unchanged waste production, because they have twice the exchange surface and the same volume.
Flattened cells have lower maximum waste-removal capacity, because their higher surface area-to-volume ratio makes waste exchange less efficient.
Flattened cells produce twice as much waste but have unchanged maximum waste-removal capacity, because production depends on surface area and removal depends on volume.

stem: A laboratory treatment removes all proteins from an isolated patch of yeast plasma membrane without disrupting its phospholipid bilayer. Carbon dioxide (CO₂) is small and nonpolar, whereas potassium (K⁺) is a small, charged ion. After treatment, how should these substances differ in their ability to pass through the membrane patch?

choices.text: CO₂ and K⁺ can both pass readily because their small size allows passage through the bilayer.
CO₂ can pass readily, whereas K⁺ passage is strongly limited by the hydrophobic core.
K⁺ can pass readily, whereas CO₂ passage is strongly limited by the hydrophilic heads.
Neither CO₂ nor K⁺ can pass readily because protein removal eliminates passage for every substance.

stem: An experimental treatment disables transport proteins in a freshwater alga’s plasma membrane but leaves its phospholipid bilayer intact. Nitrogen gas (N₂) consists of small, nonpolar molecules, whereas chloride (Cl⁻) is a small, charged ion. After treatment, which prediction about passage through this membrane is best supported?

choices.text: Cl⁻ passage is strongly restricted, while N₂ crosses readily because it can pass through the hydrophobic interior.
Cl⁻ and N₂ both cross readily because their small size allows them through the bilayer.
Cl⁻ crosses readily, while N₂ passage is strongly restricted because the membrane’s outer surfaces are hydrophilic.
Cl⁻ and N₂ are both strongly restricted because crossing the membrane always requires functioning transport proteins.

stem: In a model of membrane repair, a damaged region of a fish cell’s plasma membrane is replaced with an intact phospholipid patch that contains no proteins. Carbon dioxide (CO₂) is small and nonpolar, whereas potassium (K⁺) is a small, charged ion. Which prediction best describes passage through the replacement patch?

choices.text: Both CO₂ and K⁺ will pass readily because their small size allows them through the patch.
K⁺ will pass readily, but CO₂ passage will be strongly limited because the patch has hydrophilic outer surfaces.
Passage of both CO₂ and K⁺ will be strongly limited because neither can cross without membrane proteins.
CO₂ will pass readily, but K⁺ passage will be strongly limited by the patch’s hydrophobic interior.

stem: A laboratory is investigating recovery in yeast cells that have intact plasma membranes but initially lack cell walls. During recovery, some cells regenerate their walls, while others remain wall-free. The cells subsequently encounter conditions that drive water into them. Which prediction best describes the effect of wall regeneration?

choices.text: Cells that regenerate walls will have a higher risk of rupturing because the walls prevent unrestricted membrane expansion.
Cells that regenerate walls will have a lower risk of rupturing because the walls resist excessive expansion.
Only cells that regenerate walls will selectively restrict molecular passage because walls establish selective permeability.
Wall regeneration will leave rupture risk unchanged because plasma membranes and walls provide equivalent mechanical support.

stem: A laboratory develops a treatment that strengthens bacterial cell walls without changing the plasma membranes. Treated and untreated bacteria are exposed to conditions that drive water into the cells, causing some untreated bacteria to rupture. Which prediction about the treated bacteria is best supported?

choices.text: More treated bacteria will rupture because stronger walls prevent the unrestricted membrane expansion needed for protection.
Fewer treated bacteria will rupture because stronger walls provide greater resistance to expansion as water enters.
Treated bacteria will gain different plasma-membrane selectivity because the strengthened walls determine which molecules cross the membrane.
Treated bacteria will have the same rupture risk because their plasma membranes already provide structural support equivalent to the walls.

stem: A soil fungus encounters a chemical that makes its cell walls less rigid while leaving its plasma membranes unchanged. Following rainfall, water enters both exposed cells and unexposed cells of the same fungus. Which prediction best explains the effect of the chemical?

choices.text: Exposed cells will be less vulnerable to rupture because their more flexible walls allow greater expansion.
Exposed cells will lose selective permeability because weakened walls can no longer control passage across their plasma membranes.
Exposed cells will be more vulnerable to rupture because their weakened walls offer less resistance to expansion.
Exposed and unexposed cells will be equally vulnerable to rupture because their unchanged plasma membranes provide support equivalent to rigid walls.

stem: A freshwater algal cell initially contains an uncharged waste solute at 12 mmol/L, compared with 4 mmol/L in the surrounding water. The solute moves out of the cell through a membrane protein, with no energy supplied to the transport process. Which statement best explains this movement?

choices.text: The movement is active transport because passage through a membrane protein always consumes energy.
The movement is active transport because leaving the cell takes the solute from lower to higher concentration.
The movement is passive transport, so individual solute molecules will cease crossing the membrane when concentrations become equal.
The movement is passive transport because the solute travels from higher to lower concentration without an energy input.

stem: Researchers build artificial membrane vesicles that contain one type of transport protein and no ATP or other energy source. An uncharged sugar is at 1 mmol/L inside the vesicles and 9 mmol/L in the surrounding buffer. Over time, the sugar shows net movement into the vesicles. Which statement best explains this result?

choices.text: The sugar enters by active transport, because a transport protein must use energy to move any solute across a membrane.
The sugar enters by active transport, because moving into the vesicles carries it from lower to higher concentration.
The sugar enters by passive transport, moving from the higher concentration in the buffer to the lower concentration inside without energy input.
The sugar enters by passive transport, and sugar molecules stop crossing the membrane once the inside and outside concentrations become equal.

stem: A soil bacterium is grown in a medium containing an uncharged nutrient at 6 mmol/L, while its cytoplasm holds only 0.5 mmol/L of the nutrient. After a drug blocks all ATP production, net uptake of the nutrient through a transmembrane protein continues at the same rate. Which statement best explains why uptake continues?

choices.text: Uptake is active because any solute that passes through a transmembrane protein must be powered by energy input.
Uptake is active because moving the nutrient into the cell carries it from lower to higher concentration.
Uptake is passive because the nutrient moves from higher concentration outside to lower concentration inside, which requires no energy input.
Uptake is passive, so nutrient molecules will stop crossing the membrane once inside and outside concentrations are equal.

stem:
Freshwater amoebas are observed while cellular energy availability is low and again after energy availability returns to normal. The table summarizes membrane activity during equal observation periods.

Mean events per amoeba per 5-minute interval:
Membrane activity | Low energy | Restored energy
Plasma membrane surrounds food particles and draws them into the cell | 3 | 18
Vesicles join the plasma membrane and discharge material into the water | 7 | 28

Which interpretation accurately connects the observed changes with the transport processes involved?

choices.text: Restoring energy availability is associated with increases in both processes; food-particle engulfment is exocytosis, and vesicle discharge is endocytosis.
Restoring energy availability is associated with increases in both endocytosis and exocytosis; each process requires energy.
Food-particle engulfment requires energy, but vesicle discharge is passive transport because material leaves the cell.
Food-particle engulfment and vesicle discharge are both passive diffusion because both move material across the cell boundary.

stem:
Feeding cells in a marine sponge take in suspended bacteria and discharge cellular products into seawater. Observations are grouped by cellular energy availability, with each observation lasting 6 minutes.

Mean number of events per cell:
Membrane activity | High energy availability | Low energy availability
Plasma membrane surrounds bacteria and encloses them inside the cell | 24 | 8
Internal vesicles merge with the plasma membrane and discharge material into seawater | 15 | 5

Which interpretation correctly connects the data to the transport mechanisms?

choices.text: Both activities occur less frequently during low-energy periods; bacterial uptake is exocytosis, and vesicle-mediated discharge is endocytosis.
Bacterial uptake requires cellular energy, but vesicle-mediated discharge is passive because its cargo leaves the cell.
Both activities are diffusion and therefore passive, since each transfers material across the cell boundary.
Both endocytosis and exocytosis occur less frequently during low-energy periods, consistent with both processes requiring cellular energy.

stem:
Cultured mammalian cells were divided into two groups and observed for 15 minutes. One group was given a compound that sharply lowers ATP supply. The control group was untreated.

Mean events per cell in 15 minutes:
Membrane activity | Control | Low ATP
Plasma membrane pockets inward and encloses large external particles | 32 | 5
Internal vesicles merge with the plasma membrane and expel their contents | 50 | 9

Which statement accurately summarizes the data and names the transport processes?

choices.text: Both activities decline when ATP is limited; inward enclosure is exocytosis, and vesicle merging that expels contents is endocytosis.
Both activities decline when ATP is limited; inward enclosure is endocytosis, vesicle merging is exocytosis, and both depend on energy.
Only inward enclosure depends on energy; vesicle merging is passive because its contents leave the cell.
Both activities are passive transport, since all material crossing the plasma membrane moves by diffusion.

stem: A plant cell accumulates ions in its central vacuole. The high ion concentration inside the vacuole would disrupt metabolic reactions if that concentration also occurred in the cytoplasm. How does the vacuole membrane benefit this cell?

choices.text: It makes ion concentrations equally high in the vacuole and cytoplasm, allowing reactions in both spaces to proceed without interference.
It blocks every substance from entering or leaving the vacuole, making ion storage independent of the rest of the cell.
It provides a separate space for ion storage, reducing interference with metabolic reactions in the cytoplasm.
It adds surface area to the plasma membrane, increasing the cell’s uptake of nutrients from its surroundings.

stem: In a yeast cell, enzymes inside a membrane-bound compartment convert substance X into substance Y. Enzymes in the cytoplasm can convert Y back into X. How does the compartment membrane benefit the production of Y?

choices.text: It spreads both groups of enzymes throughout the cytoplasm so their reactions cannot interfere with one another.
It blocks every exchange of molecules with the cytoplasm so the compartment operates independently of the cell.
It enlarges the plasma membrane so the cell can absorb substances faster from its surroundings.
It separates the production of Y from cytoplasmic reactions that would convert Y back into X.

stem: In a single-celled alga, reactions inside a membrane-bound compartment use a sugar to produce a storage carbohydrate. Reactions in the cytoplasm use the same sugar to make other products. Which statement best explains how the compartment membrane can benefit storage carbohydrate production?

choices.text: It spreads both reaction sets throughout the cytoplasm, reducing competition by mixing their components uniformly.
It blocks every substance from entering or leaving, making carbohydrate production independent of the rest of the cell.
It enlarges the plasma membrane, increasing the cell’s surface area for absorbing sugar from its surroundings.
It separates the reaction sets, limiting competition for the sugar available inside the compartment.

stem:
A computer simulation models a membrane-bound compartment in a yeast cell. Enzymes attached to the compartment’s membrane carry out metabolic reactions. A remodeling step smooths out membrane folds, reducing total internal membrane area from 60 μm² to 30 μm². Cell volume and plasma membrane area remain unchanged. The number of attached enzymes per unit membrane area stays constant, and reactants remain abundant.

Which prediction best explains how remodeling affects the cell’s function?

choices.text: The compartment can support the same number of simultaneous reactions because the cell’s volume has not changed.
The cell takes up nutrients more slowly because smoothing the internal folds reduces its surface area for exchange with the surroundings.
The compartment can support fewer simultaneous reactions because the smaller internal membrane area accommodates fewer enzymes.
The compartment can support more simultaneous reactions because smoothing the folds increases the membrane area available for enzymes.

stem:
A model of a leaf cell represents lipid synthesis by enzymes attached to the smooth endoplasmic reticulum (ER). As the ER grows, its folds become more extensive and its total membrane area increases from 15 μm² to 45 μm². Cell volume and plasma membrane area remain unchanged. Enzyme density on the ER membrane stays constant, and reactants are plentiful.

Which statement best explains the functional change represented by this model?

choices.text: The cell retains the same capacity for simultaneous lipid-building reactions because its volume has not increased.
The cell gains more surface for nutrient exchange with its surroundings because the ER develops additional folds.
The ER supports fewer simultaneous lipid-building reactions because its extensive folds leave less membrane surface for enzymes.
The expanded ER can support more simultaneous lipid-building reactions because it provides attachment space for more enzymes.

stem:
A classroom model represents a mitochondrion in a human heart muscle cell. Enzymes attached to the mitochondrial inner membrane participate in ATP production. Two possible membrane layouts occupy the same mitochondrial volume:

Layout R: few folds, with 18 μm² of inner membrane.
Layout S: many folds, with 54 μm² of inner membrane.

The layouts have equal numbers of enzyme molecules per unit membrane area, and reactants are plentiful. Neither cell volume nor plasma membrane area changes between layouts. Which statement best explains the functional advantage of layout S?

choices.text: The layouts support equal numbers of simultaneous reactions involved in ATP production because their mitochondrial volumes are equal.
Layout S allows faster nutrient exchange with the cell’s surroundings because its folds enlarge the plasma membrane.
Layout S can support more simultaneous reactions involved in ATP production because its inner membrane accommodates more enzymes.
Layout S supports fewer simultaneous reactions involved in ATP production because its folds leave less membrane area for enzymes.

topic_evidence.title: Structure of Water and Hydrogen Bonding

stem: A shallow pond and the sand beside it receive the same sunlight for an hour. The sand heats up by many degrees, but the pond water warms only slightly. Which statement best explains why the water changes temperature so little?

choices.text: Water molecules are nonpolar, so they pass sunlight through without absorbing much of it and only a small fraction of the incoming heat is taken in by the pond.
Heat absorbed by the water is first used to break some of the many hydrogen bonds between polar water molecules, so less of it raises the molecules' motion and temperature.
Cohesion pulls the water molecules together at the surface, which blocks heat from entering the pond.
Evaporation removes all of the absorbed heat immediately, so the pond cannot warm at all.

stem: A chemical analysis of an unknown biological polymer finds carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, and phosphorus, but no sulfur. Which molecule is most consistent with this composition?

choices.text: A protein with many cysteine residues, because proteins contain nitrogen and sulfur.
A triglyceride, because fats are rich in carbon and hydrogen and store energy.
A cellulose chain, because it is a large polymer built from many repeating subunits and its monomers are joined into long chains by covalent bonds.
A DNA strand, because nitrogen is in its nucleotide bases and phosphorus is in the phosphate groups of its backbone.

stem: A cell links 50 amino acids into one polypeptide chain by forming peptide bonds. Which statement correctly describes the water involved?

choices.text: Forty-nine water molecules are released, one for each peptide bond formed by dehydration synthesis.
Fifty water molecules are released, one for each amino acid added.
Forty-nine water molecules are consumed, because building a polymer requires adding water.
No water is involved, because peptide bonds form by simply joining two monomers directly, which makes dehydration synthesis seem to be a simple joining reaction.

stem: A potato plant stores glucose in its tubers as starch, while its cell walls contain cellulose, also a polymer of glucose. Which statement best explains why these two carbohydrates serve different functions?

choices.text: Cellulose is built from a different monosaccharide than starch, so the two polymers cannot share a monomer.
Carbohydrates function only as energy sources, so cellulose must be used as stored fuel like starch for the whole plant, including the cell walls.
The same glucose subunits are joined in different arrangements, with branched, accessible starch suited to storage and linear cellulose suited to rigid support.
Starch is a carbohydrate made by dehydration synthesis, while cellulose forms by hydrolysis, which gives it its different role.

stem: A scientist compares two fats at 4 degrees C. Every fatty acid in Fat 1 has only single carbon-carbon bonds. Every fatty acid in Fat 2 has two carbon-carbon double bonds. Which prediction is best supported by the structure of the fatty acids?

choices.text: Fat 2 is more likely to be solid, because double bonds are stronger and hold the molecules together.
Fat 1 is more likely to be solid, because its straight chains pack tightly together.
Both fats are equally likely to be solid, because both are made of carbon and hydrogen.
Fat 2 is more likely to be solid, because it has more hydrogen atoms bonded to its carbons.

stem: One strand of a DNA segment is written 5'-ATGCCG-3'. Which is the sequence of the complementary DNA strand, written 5' to 3'?

choices.text: 5'-TACGGC-3'
5'-UACGGC-3'
5'-GCCGTA-3'
5'-CGGCAT-3'

stem: A reducing chemical breaks the disulfide bridges between cysteine side chains in a single-chain enzyme. The amino acid sequence is unchanged, but the enzyme loses its activity. Which level of protein structure is directly altered?

choices.text: Tertiary structure, because disulfide bridges between R groups help hold the polypeptide in its overall three-dimensional shape.
Primary structure, because breaking the bridges changes the order of amino acids so that the whole chain rearranges.
Secondary structure, because disulfide bridges are the main bonds in alpha helices.
Quaternary structure, because the bridges hold several polypeptide chains together.

stem: A white blood cell engulfs a bacterium into a vesicle and destroys it. Which organelle most directly carries out the destruction of the engulfed material?

choices.text: Smooth ER, because it detoxifies harmful substances in the cell and keeps the cell safe from toxins that enter.
Rough ER, because its ribosomes make proteins that attack the bacterium.
Lysosome, because it fuses with the vesicle and its hydrolytic enzymes digest the contents.
Mitochondrion, because it supplies the large amount of ATP needed for the response.

stem: A student is asked to explain how cell compartmentalization arose and how it differs between prokaryotes and eukaryotes. Which statement gives the most accurate explanation?

choices.text: Mitochondria and chloroplasts formed when the host cell's plasma membrane folded inward around parts of its own cytoplasm. Prokaryotes lack these organelles, and eukaryotes use internal membranes to partition the cell.

Mitochondria and chloroplasts descended from engulfed free-living prokaryotes. Prokaryotes have no internal organization, so all of their molecules and reactions mix freely, while eukaryotes partition the cell with internal membranes.

Because mitochondria and chloroplasts evolved from prokaryotes, modern prokaryotes also contain mitochondria and chloroplasts. Both cell types therefore compartmentalize using membrane-bound organelles.

Mitochondria and chloroplasts descended from once free-living prokaryotes that were engulfed by a host cell, which fits their double membranes. Prokaryotes typically lack membrane-bound organelles but still have specialized internal regions, while eukaryotes use internal membranes to partition the cell.

stem: Two cube-shaped cells are compared. Cell P has sides of 2 micrometers and Cell Q has sides of 4 micrometers. Which statement correctly compares their surface area-to-volume ratios?

choices.text: Both surface area and volume double, so the ratio is the same in both cells.
Cell Q's surface area is 4 times greater and its volume is 8 times greater, so its ratio is half that of Cell P.
Cell Q's surface area is 8 times greater and its volume is 4 times greater, so its ratio is twice that of Cell P.
Cell Q's surface area increases 4-fold and volume 8-fold, so its ratio is higher because 8 is greater than 4.

stem: Phospholipids are placed in water and spontaneously form a closed bilayer sphere. Which description of the arrangement is correct?

choices.text: The hydrophobic tails face the water on both surfaces, and the heads face each other in the middle so the water-loving side stays in the middle of the bilayer.
All heads and tails mix evenly throughout the sphere because the molecules move freely.
The heads of the outer layer face the tails of the inner layer so the layers stick together.
The hydrophilic phosphate heads face the water on both the outer and inner surfaces, and the hydrophobic fatty-acid tails face each other inside the bilayer.

stem: A cell is in a solution containing equal amounts of four substances, and no transport proteins for any of them are present in the membrane. Which substance would cross the phospholipid bilayer most readily?

choices.text: N2, because it is small and nonpolar and can dissolve in the hydrophobic interior of the bilayer.
Na+, because it is a very small ion.
Glucose, because the cell constantly needs it for energy and the cell would take it in as quickly as it needs.
K+, because it is moving toward a region of the cell where potassium is abundant.

stem: The concentration of an ion is 140 mM inside a cell and 4 mM outside. A membrane protein moves the ion into the cell. Which statement best describes this movement?

choices.text: It is passive transport, because a membrane protein is involved and proteins lower the energy needed.
It is facilitated diffusion, because ions are charged and charged particles always use channels.
It is active transport, because the ion moves from low to high concentration, which requires energy input, typically from ATP.

stem: The reaction glucose + phosphate to glucose-6-phosphate does not occur spontaneously. A cell couples it to ATP hydrolysis and the reaction proceeds. Why does coupling make the reaction possible?
